verse.text: Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus, to all the holy ones in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons:
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and not for a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servants.” In the Greek Old Testament “slave of the Lord” was also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David, and a first-century reader could have heard both the lowliness and the dignity.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word for all the believers in a place, as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others have “God’s people.”

The first word was an ordinary term for a supervisor or official and is plural here, so it does not yet describe a single bishop presiding over a city’s church, as the word “bishop” now implies. The second word ordinarily means a servant or assistant, but here it appears to name a recognized role in the assembly, so “deacons” is kept. What exactly either group did at Philippi is not known.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God every time I remember you,
always, in every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy,
because of your partnership in the good news from the first day until now,
verse.note: “Gospel” has become a religious term and the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

The Greek word means having something in common and was used of business partnerships as well as friendships. Here it refers to the Philippians’ active share in Paul’s work, including their financial support (4:15), so “partnership” is used in place of the older “fellowship,” as in many modern versions. The related word in verse 7 is rendered “partners.”

verse.text: being confident of this very thing, that the one who began a good work in you will carry it through to completion, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.

It is right for me to think this way about all of you, because I hold you in my heart, since all of you are partners with me in grace, both in my chains and in the defense and confirmation of the good news.

note.term: I hold you in my heart
note.traditional: I have you in my heart

verse.note: The Greek can also be read “you hold me in your heart,” since both pronouns are in the same case. The word order favors the rendering in the text, which most translations follow, but a minority of versions and scholars take it the other way.

The adjective normally rendered “righteous” or “just” is used here in the everyday impersonal expression “it is right,” meaning proper or fitting. Neither “righteous” nor “just” would be natural English in this construction.

verse.text: For God is my witness how I long for all of you with the deep affection of Christ Jesus.
And this I pray: that your love may overflow still more and more in knowledge and every kind of insight,
so that you can discern what matters most, in order to be sincere and blameless for the day of Christ,
filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verse.note: The phrase can mean the fruit that consists of righteousness or the fruit that righteousness produces, that is, conduct flowing from a right standing with God; the Greek does not decide. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice), so “righteousness” here covers both being in the right and doing what is right.

verse.text: Now I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has actually turned out for the progress of the good news,
so that it has become clear to the whole imperial guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ,

note.traditional: the whole praetorian guard; the palace

verse.note: The Greek is a Latin loanword, praetorium. It could mean a governor’s official residence, as in the Gospels and Acts, or the emperor’s elite guard in Rome. The following “and to everyone else” suggests people, not a building, so most modern translations take it as the guard. The choice is tied to the disputed question of where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote.

verse.text: and most of the brothers and sisters, made confident in the Lord by my chains, dare all the more to speak the word without fear.
verse.note: Many early manuscripts read “the word of God,” and a few “the word of the Lord.” The shorter reading is the one printed in the Greek text translated here, and the longer forms may be scribal clarifications, though the manuscript evidence for “of God” is strong and editors are divided.

verse.text: Some, it is true, preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.
The latter do so out of love, knowing that I am placed here for the defense of the good news;
the former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not from pure motives, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains.
What of it? Only this: in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,
for I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the support of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,
verse.note: The Greek word can mean rescue from danger or salvation in the full sense, and many modern versions have “deliverance,” understanding release from prison. Paul’s words here match the Greek version of Job 13:16, where Job expects to be vindicated before God, and verse 20 expects this outcome “whether through life or through death.” Many scholars therefore think Paul means his final vindication, not simply his release; the same word is used in verse 28.

verse.text: in keeping with my eager expectation and hope that I will be put to shame in nothing, but that with all boldness, now as always, Christ will be exalted in my body, whether through life or through death.
For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.
But if I am to live on in the flesh, that means fruit from my labor—and which I will choose I do not know.

note.term: that means fruit from my labor
note.traditional: this is the fruit of my labour

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and seems to break off mid-sentence. It can also be read as one sentence: “But if living on in the flesh means fruitful labor for me, then I do not know which to choose.” The verb rendered “know” usually means “make known” elsewhere in the New Testament, so “I cannot tell” is also possible.

verse.text: I am hard pressed between the two: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is better by far;
but to stay on in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.
And confident of this, I know that I will stay, and stay alongside all of you, for your progress and joy in the faith,
so that your boasting in Christ Jesus may overflow because of me, through my presence with you again.

Only live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear about you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one soul contending side by side for the faith of the good news,

note.traditional: conduct yourselves; let your manner of life be

verse.note: The verb comes from civic life and means to live as a citizen and fulfill a citizen’s obligations, though in Jewish Greek it could also mean simply to live by a certain way of life. Philippi was a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, and Paul returns to the image in 3:20. Most commentators think the civic sense is intended, though translations usually render it generally.

Many versions have “one mind”; the Greek word is the one for a person’s life or inner self, and the phrase describes a community acting as if it shared a single self. The preceding “in one spirit” could also be read “in the one Spirit,” referring to God’s Spirit, but the parallel with “one soul” favors the sense of united resolve.

verse.text: and in no way frightened by your opponents. This is a sign to them of destruction, but of your salvation, and this is from God.
For it has been granted to you, for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake,
having the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear of in me.
So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion,
verse.note: The Greek word means having something in common and is stronger than modern “fellowship” may suggest. The phrase can mean a bond among believers that the Spirit creates, or a shared participation in the Spirit; many recent versions and scholars prefer “sharing in the Spirit.” The rendering leaves both open and matches the same phrase in 2 Corinthians 13:13.

verse.text: make my joy complete by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul, of one mind,
doing nothing out of selfish ambition or empty conceit, but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves,
each of you looking not only to your own interests but also to the interests of others.
Have this mind among yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus,

note.term: which was also in Christ Jesus
note.traditional: which was also in Christ Jesus

verse.note: The Greek clause has no verb. The traditional reading supplies “was,” making Christ’s own attitude the model. Many scholars instead supply “you have,” giving “which you also have in Christ Jesus,” that is, the mindset that belongs to those who are in Christ. Both readings are well supported.

verse.text: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be exploited,
verse.note: The word denotes the visible form by which something is recognized, not a disguise; it is repeated in “the form of a slave” in verse 7. Interpreters differ on whether it points here to divine nature, divine glory, or divine status. Verses 6–11 are widely thought to be an early hymn or a passage of elevated prose, whether Paul is quoting it or composed it himself.

This rare noun has been read as something seized (older versions have “robbery”), something to be seized, or something to be clung to. Studies of the idiom with verbs of considering indicate that it means something to take advantage of, and several modern versions follow this. On that reading Christ already had equality with God and did not use it for his own gain; “a thing to be grasped” leaves open that he did not yet have it.

verse.text: but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, coming to be in the likeness of human beings. And being found in appearance as a human being,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by another, and the contrast with “Lord” in verse 11 depends on it. Most English versions soften it to “servant,” though some have “slave.” The related verb in verse 22 is rendered “served with me as a slave.”

verse.text: he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name,
so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verse.note: Verses 10–11 echo Isaiah 45:23, where God declares that every knee will bend to him and every tongue swear allegiance. In the Greek Scriptures “Lord” regularly stands in for the divine name, so many interpreters take “the name that is above every name” to be “Lord.” Language used there of Israel’s God alone is here applied to Jesus, to the Father’s glory.

verse.text: So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only as in my presence but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,
for it is God who works in you both the willing and the working, for his good pleasure.
Do everything without grumbling or arguing,
so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world,
holding fast to the word of life, so that on the day of Christ I may boast that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.

note.term: holding fast to the word of life
note.traditional: holding forth the word of life

verse.note: The verb can mean either “hold fast” or “hold out, offer.” Most recent versions and commentators prefer “hold fast,” which suits the call to stay blameless amid opposition. The older rendering “holding forth” would make the phrase describe the Philippians offering the message to others, which the image of shining lights could also support.

verse.text: But even if I am being poured out as a drink offering over the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and I rejoice with all of you.

note.term: poured out as a drink offering
note.traditional: poured out as a drink offering

verse.note: In both Jewish and Greek worship, wine was poured out beside or over a sacrifice to complete it. Paul pictures the Philippians’ faith as the main offering and his own possible death as the libation added to it. The word rendered “service” was used in the Greek Scriptures for priestly ministry.

verse.text: In the same way you also should rejoice, and rejoice with me.
I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be heartened when I learn how things are with you.
For I have no one of kindred soul who will genuinely care about how things are with you,
verse.note: The rare adjective means “of equal soul.” It may mean that no one else shares Paul’s own outlook as Timothy does, or that Paul has no one else like Timothy; English versions divide between the two. It is one of several compounds of the word for “soul” in this chapter (also in verses 2 and 19).

verse.text: for they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.
But you know his proven character, how like a child with a father he has served with me as a slave for the good news.
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: So I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how things will go with me,
and I am confident in the Lord that I myself will also come soon.
But I have considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you—my brother and coworker and fellow soldier, and your envoy and minister to my need—
verse.note: The Greek word is the one elsewhere rendered “apostle.” Here it has its ordinary sense of a delegate sent by others: the Philippian church sent Epaphroditus to Paul with their gift (4:18). Most versions have “messenger”; “envoy” is used because he was sent to act on the church’s behalf, not only to carry a message.

verse.text: since he has been longing for all of you and has been distressed because you heard that he was sick.
Indeed he was sick, close to death. But God had mercy on him, and not on him only but on me also, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow.
So I am sending him all the more eagerly, so that you may rejoice at seeing him again and I may be less sorrowful.
verse.note: The Greek verbs here and in verse 25 are past tenses, written from the standpoint of the readers when they receive the letter, a common convention in ancient letters. Epaphroditus was most likely the one carrying this letter, so English uses the present. Older versions have “I sent.”

verse.text: So welcome him in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor,
because he came close to death for the work of Christ, risking his life to make up what was lacking in your service to me.
Finally, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble for me, and for you it is a safeguard.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole community at Philippi, which included women he names in the next chapter. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render as here.

verse.text: Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for the mutilation.

note.traditional: the concision; the mutilation; those who mutilate the flesh

verse.note: Paul plays on two similar words: katatomē (“cutting up, mutilation”) here and peritomē (“circumcision”) in the next verse. He refuses the honored name to those who insist that non-Jewish believers be circumcised, and uses instead a word whose verb in the Greek Old Testament describes forbidden pagan gashing of the body. “Dogs” was a common term of contempt, here turned on these teachers.

verse.text: For we are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God and boast in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh,

note.term: worship by the Spirit of God

verse.note: The earliest and most widespread manuscripts read “of God” (worship by the Spirit of God). Others read “God” as the object, giving “worship God in spirit,” which lies behind the King James rendering. Most modern editions and translations follow the reading translated here.

verse.text: though I myself have grounds for confidence in the flesh as well. If anyone else thinks they can put confidence in the flesh, I can do so more:
circumcised on the eighth day, from the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;
as to zeal, a persecutor of the assembly; as to the righteousness that is in the law, found blameless.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a citizens’ gathering and the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or institution. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere so that the reader can see it is one word.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, and the verb “justify.” The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God’s action to set things right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness”; the traditional word is kept here and in verse nine.

verse.text: But whatever were gains to me, these I have come to count as loss because of Christ.

More than that, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of everything, and I count it dung, so that I may gain Christ
verse.note: The word was used both for excrement and for refuse such as table scraps or sweepings, and it carried a note of disgust. Most modern versions choose “rubbish” or “garbage”; the King James has “dung.” Either is lexically sound; the stronger word is used here because the term was not a polite one.

verse.text: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the one that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that rests on faith,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “faith of Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: the believer’s faith in Christ, or Christ’s own faithfulness. “Faith in Christ” is the traditional and still majority reading and is followed here. “The faithfulness of Christ” has substantial scholarly support and would make the phrase refer to Christ’s obedient death, with the believer’s faith mentioned at the end of the verse.

verse.text: so that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and a sharing in his sufferings, being conformed to his death,
if somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.
Not that I have already obtained this or have already been made perfect, but I press on, if only I may take hold of it, because I was myself taken hold of by Christ.
verse.note: The Greek connective can mean “because” or “that for which.” On the second reading Paul presses on to take hold of the very thing for which Christ took hold of him. Translations and commentators are divided. The same verb, “take hold of,” is used for Paul’s striving and for Christ’s seizing of him.

verse.text: Brothers and sisters, I do not consider myself to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what is behind and stretching out toward what is ahead,
I press on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

note.traditional: the high calling; the upward call; called me heavenward

verse.note: The phrase is literally “the above call.” It may mean a call that comes from above, a call that summons upward to heaven, or, continuing the athletic image, the summons of the victor to receive the prize. The rendering leaves these open.

verse.text: So let all of us who are mature be of this mind; and if on any point you are of a different mind, this too God will reveal to you.
verse.note: This adjective belongs to the same word-family as “made perfect” in verse twelve, and Greek readers would have heard the echo. It commonly meant full-grown or adult, and that is the likely sense here. Some think Paul is using the word with irony, borrowing a claim to be “perfect” made by others.

verse.text: Only, whatever point we have reached, let us keep in step with that.
Join together in imitating me, brothers and sisters, and keep your eyes on those who walk in this way, according to the pattern you have in us.
For many are walking—I often told you about them, and now I say it even in tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame; their minds are on earthly things.
For our commonwealth is in the heavens, and from it we eagerly await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verse.note: In the period the word regularly meant a state or civic body, including a colony of people living abroad under their home city’s constitution, rather than the abstract status of citizenship. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens belonged to Rome though they lived far from it, and “savior” and “lord” were titles given to the emperor. Most versions have “citizenship,” which conveys the point well enough; “commonwealth” is closer to attested usage and fits “from it” that follows.

The Greek is plural, a turn of phrase carried over from Hebrew and Aramaic. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; this translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it and God’s dwelling is meant.

verse.text: who will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory, in keeping with the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.
So then, my brothers and sisters, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and the next verse speaks directly to two women in the community. “Brothers” alone would now suggest that only men are addressed. Many modern translations make the same choice; more literal ones keep “brothers” with a footnote.

verse.text: I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord.
Yes, and I ask you too, true companion, help these women, who struggled alongside me in the good news, together with Clement and the rest of my coworkers, whose names are in the book of life.
verse.note: The Greek word means someone yoked together with another, a partner or comrade. It may be a description of an unnamed colleague, or a proper name, Syzygus, with Paul playing on its meaning (“Syzygus, rightly so called”). The name is not attested elsewhere, so most translations take it as a description, but the identity of the person is unknown.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term or the name of a book, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news”.

verse.text: Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!
Let your gentleness be known to all people. The Lord is near.
verse.note: The Greek can mean near in time (the Lord’s coming is close, as in 3:20) or near in presence (the Lord is close to those who call on him, echoing the Psalms). Interpreters are divided, and Paul may intend both. The sentence can also be attached either to the call for gentleness before it or to the call not to be anxious after it.

verse.text: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

Finally, brothers and sisters, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is well spoken of—if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise—think about these things.
What you learned and received and heard and saw in me—practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your concern for me has bloomed again; you were in fact concerned, but you had no opportunity.
Not that I say this out of want, for I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am in.
verse.note: The Greek word was a favorite term of Stoic and Cynic philosophers for the self-sufficiency of the wise person who needs nothing from outside. Paul borrows the term but relocates its source: verse 13 makes clear that his sufficiency comes from the one who empowers him, not from himself.

verse.text: I know how to be brought low, and I know how to have more than enough. In anything and everything I have learned the secret—both to be well fed and to go hungry, both to have more than enough and to be in want.

note.traditional: I am instructed / I have learned the secret

verse.note: The verb, used only here in the New Testament, was the technical term for being initiated into the mystery religions. Paul uses it figuratively: his initiation has been into living with plenty and with hunger alike.

verse.text: I have strength for everything in the one who empowers me.

note.term: I have strength for everything in the one who empowers me
note.traditional: I can do all things through him who strengthens me

verse.note: The verb means to be strong or to have strength for something, and “everything” refers back to the circumstances just listed—plenty and hunger, abundance and want. The traditional wording is often heard as a promise of unlimited achievement; the context is endurance in every situation. Later manuscripts add “Christ” to identify the one who empowers, which is the reading behind the King James Version.

verse.text: Still, you did well to share with me in my affliction.
You Philippians yourselves also know that in the early days of the good news, when I left Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in an account of giving and receiving except you alone;
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and its reference is clear, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

note.term: an account of giving and receiving
note.traditional: in the matter of giving and receiving

verse.note: Paul uses the language of commerce throughout verses 15–18. “Account,” “giving and receiving” (credit and debit), “fruit” (which could also mean profit or interest), “increases,” and “received payment in full” (the wording of a receipt) were all familiar from business dealings. He describes the Philippians’ gifts as a partnership whose real profit accrues to them.

verse.text: for even in Thessalonica you sent something for my need more than once.
Not that I seek the gift; rather, I seek the fruit that increases to your account.
I have received payment in full and have more than enough. I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent—a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

note.traditional: an odour of a sweet smell / a fragrant offering

verse.note: This phrase is the Septuagint’s standard expression for the smell of a sacrifice rising to God and pleasing him, used from Genesis 8:21 onward and often in Leviticus. Paul moves from the language of the ledger to the language of the altar: the gift sent to him is really an offering to God.

verse.text: And my God will fill every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
To our God and Father be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus. The brothers and sisters who are with me greet you.
verse.note: The word is used of every member of the community as someone set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saint” now suggests a canonized individual or a person of exceptional virtue, which is not the meaning. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people”.

verse.text: All the holy ones greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household.
verse.note: This does not mean the emperor’s relatives. The phrase covered the large body of slaves and freed slaves in the imperial service, who staffed the administration in Rome and in the provinces. Where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote is disputed (Rome is the traditional view; Ephesus and Caesarea are also proposed), and members of the imperial service were found in all of these places.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
